common_name: Mokka Coffee (Maui Mokka, Low-Caffeine Dwarf Coffee)

planting.note: Plant container-grown seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with light shade; Mokka is an extremely compact, hedge-like dwarf coffee well suited to container culture.

directions: Mokka arose as a naturally occurring dwarf mutation of Bourbon and has been cultivated since at least the early twentieth century, prized for a compact, densely branched habit that looks more like a clipped hedge than a typical coffee tree. Its narrow leaves and diminutive cherries yield beans containing roughly half the caffeine of standard arabica cultivars, while still producing a heavy-bodied, chocolaty cup often noted for dried-fruit and spice character, especially when natural-processed. The naturally short internodes keep mature plants under six feet, making it one of the few coffee selections well suited to large-container or patio growing outside true tropical climates. Give it the same rich, humus-heavy, slightly acidic soil and filtered light preferred by other arabica types, and expect several years of growth before the first useful harvest.
sources: World Coffee Research Arabica Coffee Varieties Catalog

common_name: Pache Común Coffee (Pache Comun, Guatemalan Dwarf Typica)

planting.note: Plant container-grown seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil with filtered shade; Pache Común is a naturally dwarf, single-gene mutation of Typica first identified in Guatemala.

directions: Pache Común is a spontaneous dwarf mutation of Typica first documented at Finca El Brito in Guatemala, where a single recessive gene compresses internode length and produces a noticeably shorter, more compact tree than standard Typica. That reduced stature lets growers plant it at higher density and harvest more easily by hand, without sacrificing the clean, balanced, classically Typica-like cup quality the variety is known for. It remains one of the most widely planted arabica selections in Guatemala's highland coffee zones, typically grown alongside Caturra and Catuaí under similar management. Provide rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, filtered overhead shade, and consistent moisture, and expect a first meaningful harvest roughly three to four years after transplanting.
sources: World Coffee Research Arabica Coffee Varieties Catalog

planting.note: Plant container-grown seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with filtered shade; Pache Colís is an even more compact dwarf than either of its Caturra and Pache Común parents.

directions: Pache Colís is a deliberate cross between Caturra and Pache Común, combining two separate dwarfing lineages into a plant that grows even shorter and more compact than either parent. The extremely reduced stature suits very high density plantings and easy hand-picking, characteristics that made it popular among Guatemalan smallholders looking to maximize yield on limited land. Cup quality tracks closely with its Typica- and Bourbon-derived parentage, generally clean and well balanced rather than especially distinctive. Grow it exactly as you would other compact arabica selections, in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with filtered shade and steady moisture.
sources: World Coffee Research Arabica Coffee Varieties Catalog

common_name: Colombia Coffee Variety (Cenicafé Rust-Resistant Caturra Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with filtered shade; the Colombia variety is a compact, Caturra-type selection bred for durable leaf-rust resistance.

directions: Released in 1980 by Colombia's national coffee research center, Cenicafé, the Colombia variety was bred to combine durable resistance to coffee leaf rust with the large bean size, high productivity, and good cup quality growers expect from a Caturra-type plant. Its rust resistance traces back to the naturally occurring Timor Hybrid, an interspecific cross between arabica and robusta that was, at the time, the only known reliable source of resistance genes for arabica breeding programs. The variety keeps a compact, short-statured growth habit similar to Caturra, allowing dense planting and straightforward hand-harvesting. It became a cornerstone of Colombian coffee agriculture for two decades before newer rust-resistant releases such as Castillo largely superseded it. Cultivate it with the same rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and filtered shade recommended for other compact arabica types.
sources: Cenicafé (Colombian National Center for Coffee Research)
World Coffee Research Arabica Coffee Varieties Catalog

planting.note: Plant container-grown seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil with filtered shade; Tabi grows taller and more open than dwarf Caturra-type selections.

directions: Tabi is a three-way cross of Typica, Bourbon, and Timor Hybrid released by Cenicafé in 2002; its name means "good" in the Guambiano language of southwestern Colombia. The Timor Hybrid parentage contributes durable resistance to coffee leaf rust, while Bourbon lends sweetness and rounded acidity and Typica adds clarity and refinement to the cup, giving Tabi a reputation for above-average quality among rust-resistant varieties. Cherries are large and elongated, ripening slowly at higher elevations where the extra time on the tree helps build sugars and organic acids. Plants grow taller and more open than dwarf Caturra-type selections, closer in stature to Typica and Bourbon. Provide rich, moist, well-drained soil, filtered shade, and protection from temperatures below 55°F.
sources: Cenicafé (Colombian National Center for Coffee Research)
World Coffee Research Arabica Coffee Varieties Catalog

planting.note: Plant container-grown seedlings in spring in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with filtered shade; Sidra is an unusually vigorous, thick-trunked arabica that grows taller than most dwarf cultivars.

directions: Sidra rose to prominence on farms in Ecuador's Pichincha province before spreading into Colombia's specialty coffee scene during the 2010s. Its exact parentage is debated: growers have long described it as a cross of Typica and Red Bourbon, while genetic testing on some material points instead to Ethiopian landrace ancestry, and both explanations may apply to different Sidra populations now in circulation. The plant is notably vigorous, with an unusually thick trunk and a mature height well above compact dwarf cultivars, typically grown at 1,650-1,800 meters elevation. It has earned a following among specialty roasters for a complex, floral, fruit-forward cup that stands out in competition lots. Grow it in rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with filtered shade, allowing extra room for its taller, more vigorous habit compared with dwarf varieties like Caturra or Pacas.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in part shade to full sun; Conilon is the dominant Coffea canephora selection grown in Brazil's Espírito Santo state.

directions: Conilon, also called Kouilou, is the principal cultivated form of Coffea canephora in Brazil, where it accounts for the great majority of the country's robusta production, concentrated in the state of Espírito Santo. Compared with wild-type robusta populations it grows as a smaller, more manageable shrub, tolerates drought and heat better than most coffee types, and thrives at lower elevations than arabica requires, but it remains considerably more susceptible to coffee leaf rust than other canephora selections. Beans are valued mainly for blends, instant coffee, and the crema they add to espresso rather than for delicate cup complexity. Because it tolerates more direct sun than arabica, it can be grown with less overhead shading, though afternoon shade is still helpful in the hottest climates. Give it warm, humid conditions, fertile well-drained soil, and steady moisture through the growing season.

common_name: ICS 95 Cacao (Imperial College Selection 95, CCN-51 Parent)

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; ICS 95 is a frost-tender tropical tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: ICS 95 belongs to the historic Imperial College Selection series of Trinitario clones developed in Trinidad in the early twentieth century, combining genetic contributions from Criollo and Lower Amazon Forastero. It is best known today as one of the parent clones, alongside IMC 67, used to create the high-yielding CCN-51 hybrid that now dominates much of Ecuador's cacao production, though ICS 95 is also grown and studied in its own right for its agronomic performance and flavor contribution. Growth habit is vigorous and upright, typical of Trinitario-type selections, with moderate disease tolerance compared with pure Criollo lines. Cultivate it beneath taller shade trees in rich, moist, well-drained soil, providing the same warm, humid, sheltered conditions favored by other heirloom and hybrid cacao types.
sources: Cocoa Research Centre, University of the West Indies
PMC - Theobroma cacao L. cultivar CCN 51: a comprehensive review

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; ICS 6 is a frost-tender tropical tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: ICS 6 is another member of the Imperial College Selection series bred in Trinidad from Criollo and Lower Amazon Forastero parentage, part of the same twentieth-century breeding program that produced ICS 1 and ICS 95. It has long been maintained in cacao germplasm collections and used in breeding and comparative agronomy trials for traits including yield, vigor, and disease response, and it is occasionally planted directly for its Trinitario-type flavor contribution. Habit is moderately vigorous and upright, similar to its sister ICS selections. Provide the same filtered shade beneath taller companion trees and rich, moist, well-drained soil recommended for other Trinitario cacao types.
sources: Cocoa Research Centre, University of the West Indies, Trinidad

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade beneath taller companion trees; SCA 12 is a frost-tender tropical tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: SCA 12 is a cacao accession collected in Peru that, together with its sister clone SCA 6, has served for decades as a primary reference source of resistance to witches' broom disease (Moniliophthora perniciosa), one of the most damaging fungal diseases affecting cacao in the Americas. Breeders have used SCA 12 as a parent in a very large share of the improved, disease-resistant cacao varieties held in international germplasm collections, though its resistance has shown regional variability and has occasionally broken down against certain local disease strains. Growth habit is vigorous and upright, similar to other resistant breeding clones. Because it is grown mainly for breeding and disease-resistance trials rather than fine flavor, home growers plant it more for genetic interest than eating quality; provide it with the same filtered shade, rich moist soil, and warm humid conditions used for other cacao selections.
sources: Plant Breeding journal - Sources of resistance to witches' broom disease in cacao

planting.note: Plant stem cuttings with at least 3 nodes in moist, well-drained, organic, slightly acidic bark or orchid mix in bright indirect light with a sturdy support for aerial roots and climbing growth; Handa is a patented Vanilla planifolia selection bred for disease resistance and improved pod handling.

directions: Handa was bred by CIRAD, the French Agricultural Research Centre for International Development, on Réunion Island from a self-pollinated seedling selected for disease resistance and improved agronomic performance rather than as an ornamental novelty. It shows useful resistance to Fusarium oxysporum root and stem rot, a soil-borne disease that has damaged vanilla plantations worldwide, and produces thicker, darker green leaves along with heavier, rounder pods than standard planifolia stock. Unlike ordinary vanilla, its pods stay closed at maturity instead of splitting open, which reduces harvest losses and makes curing easier, even though vanillin content per pod runs somewhat lower than traditional stock, a tradeoff offset by higher overall yield per vine. Like all cultivated vanilla it is a climbing hemi-epiphytic orchid that must be trained up a support tree, pole, or trellis and pollinated by hand within hours of each flower opening, since its natural pollinator is absent outside Mesoamerica. Grow it in bright, filtered light and high humidity, in a loose, fast-draining orchid or bark-based medium, with warmth above 60°F year-round.
sources: CIRAD (French Agricultural Research Centre for International Development)
University of Florida IFAS Extension - Vanilla Growing in South Florida
